subject: Anatomy
summary: The thalamus is a paired deep gray‑matter structure that relays sensory and motor information to the cortex and regulates consciousness. Damage produces characteristic sensory, motor and cognitive deficits.

sections.p: The thalamus sits atop the brainstem, forming the main hub between subcortical nuclei and the cerebral cortex. It processes all modalities except smell and contributes to sleep‑wake cycles.
b: Acts as a ‘relay station’ for sensory, motor and limbic pathways
Contains multiple nuclei with distinct cortical targets

sections.p: Each thalamus is an ovoid mass of gray matter within the diencephalon, bounded laterally by the internal capsule and medially by the third ventricle.
b: Divided into anterior, medial, lateral, intralaminar and posterior nuclear groups
Each nucleus has specific afferent and efferent connections

sections.p: Anteriorly the thalamus contacts the hypothalamus; laterally it is separated from the caudate nucleus by the internal capsule; posteriorly it abuts the pulvinar and the midbrain tectum.
b: Mammillary bodies lie ventrally and are part of the limbic circuit

sections.p: Arterial supply comes from branches of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and the posterior communicating artery; deep penetrating thalamic arteries have minimal collateral flow.
b: Paramedian thalamic arteries supply medial nuclei

sections.p: Afferents arrive via spinothalamic, medial lemniscal, cerebellothalamic, and limbic pathways; efferents leave as thalamocortical radiations (internal capsule).
b: Thalamic nuclei project to specific cortical Brodmann areas

sections.p: Each nucleus filters and modulates incoming signals before sending them to the cortex, influencing perception, movement planning, attention and consciousness.
Thalamic lesions produce sensory loss, thalamic pain syndrome, movement disorders, and altered consciousness. Small‑vessel disease, hypertension, and thiamine deficiency are common causes worldwide.
b: Charcot‑Bouchard microaneurysm rupture → acute thalamic hemorrhage
Wernicke’s encephalopathy → mammillary body and medial thalamic damage
Thalamic infarct (PCA territory) → contralateral sensory loss and hemiparesis

t.b: Detects acute hemorrhage; hyperdense thalamic region confirms bleed
Identifies early ischemic thalamic infarct; restricted diffusion indicates viable tissue
Low level supports Wernicke’s; treat empirically if unavailable

sections.p: Remember the thalamus is the only deep gray structure with virtually no collateral blood flow; any small‑vessel hypertension‑related bleed here is a neurosurgical emergency.
b: Thalamic pain syndrome = chronic, burning pain after a thalamic stroke
Lesion of ventral lateral nucleus → dysmetria and intention tremor
Bilateral thalamic lesions can cause coma

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness or coma
Acute severe headache with vomiting suggesting thalamic hemorrhage
Rapidly progressive confusion in a malnourished patient (possible Wernicke’s)

faq.q: Why does a thalamic stroke cause sensory loss on the opposite side?
faq.a: Sensory fibers cross in the brainstem before reaching the ventral posterior nucleus, so a unilateral thalamic lesion affects contralateral sensation.
A chronic, burning pain that appears weeks after a thalamic infarct, due to maladaptive de‑synchronisation of sensory pathways.

faq.q: How is Wernicke’s encephalopathy related to the thalamus?
faq.a: Thiamine deficiency damages the medial thalamus and mammillary bodies, producing confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia.

exam: Explain how a lesion in the ventral posterior nucleus presents clinically and why.
Describe the arterial supply of the thalamus and the implications of its limited collateral flow.
List three common causes of thalamic injury in low‑resource settings and the key emergency management steps.
